unit.title: Risk management
unit.description: How much to risk, where to put the stop and how to tell if a system makes money

u24l1.title: Why risk matters more than being right

steps.title: The professional's question
steps.body:
Beginners ask «what should I buy?» and «will it go up?». Professionals ask: **«how much do I lose if I'm wrong?»**.

Nobody knows whether a specific trade will work out. The only thing you control 100 % is **how much you risk** on each one.

steps.title: Ten losses in a row
steps.body:
It happens even with a good system. What you have left depending on what you risk per trade:

• 1 %: you keep **90.4 %** (you recover with +10.6 %)
• 2 %: 81.7 % (+22.4 %)
• 5 %: 59.9 % (+67 %)
• 10 %: **34.9 %** (+187 %)

At 1 %, ten losses are a bad month. At 10 %, they're the end.

steps.title: What it takes to get back
steps.body: Move the loss and see how much you'd need to gain afterwards to be back where you started.
steps.tip: Big losses aren't fixed by a gain of the same size.

steps.title: Survive first
steps.body: You can be right 60 % of the time and go broke, or be right 40 % of the time and make money. The difference is how much you win when you're right and how much you lose when you're wrong.
steps.key: A trader's first goal is to survive, so that their edge, if they have one, can play out.
steps.tip: You don't control whether you're right. You control how much you lose when you're wrong.

steps.title: Play with the fall
steps.body: Raise the loss bit by bit: up to 20 % the difference is barely noticeable; from 50 % onwards it shoots up.
steps.tip: A share that falls 90 % has to multiply by ten to get back.

steps.title: Averages are misleading
steps.body:
+50 % one year and −50 % the next isn't a 0 % average: €100 → €150 → €75. You've lost 25 %.

And with 1:5 leverage, a 20 % fall in the asset wipes out 100 % of your money.
steps.key: Avoiding big losses matters more than chasing big gains.
steps.tip: Losing 50 % means you need to gain 100 %. Protect what you have first.

steps.title: What the rule says
steps.body:
If your stop is hit, you lose no more than **1 % of your capital**.

With €10,000, 1 % is **€100**. That doesn't mean investing €100: it means that, if you're wrong, you lose €100 at most.

**Size = (capital × % risk) ÷ (entry − stop)**

steps.title: Try the rule
steps.body: Leave the risk at 1 % and change the distance to the stop: watch how the amount invested changes while the maximum loss stays the same.
steps.tip: Stop close: you buy more. Stop far: you buy less. You risk the same.

steps.title: Limits that add up
steps.body: Most professionals risk between **0.5 % and 2 %** per trade; to start with, 1 % or less. It's also wise to cap your **total open risk** (no more than 5–6 % at once) and the **weight of each position** (E-Trading warns you from 20 %).
steps.key: Risk isn't the same as the amount invested: you can invest 16 % and risk 1 %.
steps.tip: First you decide where you're wrong. Then how many shares you buy.

steps.title: Step by step
steps.body:
1. Capital: **€10,000**. 1 % risk = **€100**.
2. Entry **€50**, stop **€47**: a distance of **€3** per share.
3. Size: 100 ÷ 3 = **33 shares** (about €1,650).

If the stop is hit you lose 33 × 3 = €99: 1 % of the account, even though you've invested 16.5 %.

steps.title: Work out your size
steps.body: Enter €10,000, 1 % risk, an entry at €50 and the stop 6 % away (about €3). Then move the stop out to 10 % and watch the size drop.
steps.tip: The more volatile asset needs a wider stop and, therefore, fewer shares.

steps.title: Key takeaway
steps.body: With a stop €1 away you could buy 100 shares; with one €10 away, only 10. Both trades risk €100. That way every trade carries the same weight, whatever the asset.
steps.key: You don't decide how much you buy: the distance to your stop does.
steps.tip: Always round down: better to risk €99 than €102.

u24l5.title: Where to put the stop loss

steps.title: Three methods
steps.body:
1. **Structural:** on the other side of a level. If you buy at a support, below the support or below the low of the reversal candle.
2. **Volatility-based:** 2–3 times the **ATR** (the average range of the last 14 candles), so the noise doesn't knock you out.
3. **Time-based:** if, say, after 10 sessions it hasn't done what you expected, you get out.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
• Stop too close: the noise knocks you out.
• On obvious round numbers (€50.00): that's where everyone else's are.
• **Moving it further away** as the price gets close: a small loss turns into a big one.
• Not setting one «because it'll bounce back».

And watch out: with a price gap, the stop fills worse than planned.

steps.title: The golden rule
steps.body: If the trade goes your way, you can raise the stop: to the entry price or below the latest higher low. But you never move it further away against you.
steps.key: The stop goes where your idea stops being valid, not where losing starts to hurt.
steps.tip: The stop isn't where it hurts: it's where your idea dies.

u24l6.title: Thinking in R: risk and reward

steps.title: What R is
steps.body:
**1R** is what you risk on a trade: distance to the stop × number of shares. If you risk €100:

• Stop hit: **−1R**.
• You win €250: **+2.5R**.
• You exit early losing €40: **−0.4R**.

Measuring in R lets you compare trades of any size.

steps.title: Reward/risk
steps.body:
Before entering, compare the distance to the **target** with the distance to the **stop**.

Entry €50, stop €47 (€3 risk), target €59 (€9 reward): a **3:1** ratio.

Many traders won't enter below **2:1**.

steps.title: Key takeaway
steps.body: If you risk €100 and win €300, you've made 3R. If you risk €50 and win €150, that's also 3R: both trades were equally good.
steps.key: A trade is measured in multiples of what you risked.

steps.title: The formula
steps.body:
**Expectancy (in R) = (win rate × average win) − (loss rate × average loss)**

• A: 40 % win rate, wins 2R → 0.4 × 2 − 0.6 × 1 = **+0.2R** ✓
• B: 60 %, wins 0.5R → 0.6 × 0.5 − 0.4 × 1 = **−0.1R** ✗
• C: 30 %, wins 3R → **+0.2R** ✓
• D: 50 %, wins 1R → **0** (negative after costs) ✗

steps.title: Costs
steps.body:
Every trade pays commission, *spread* and, if there's leverage, financing.

If your expectancy is +0.1R and costs are 0.15R per trade, your real system **loses**. The more trades you make, the more they weigh.

steps.title: How much you could make
steps.body: With +0.2R, 1 % risk and 100 trades a year you'd get about 20R: close to 20 % a year, with losing streaks along the way. It's just an example, not a promise: an edge like that is already very good and hard to keep.
steps.key: A system makes money if, on average, each trade wins more than it loses, counting both wins and losses.
steps.tip: You don't need to be right often: you need your wins to be worth more than your losses.

u24l1-1.prompt: What's the only thing you control 100 % on every trade?
options: Whether the price will go up
How much you risk if you're wrong
u24l1-1.explanation: Nobody knows how a specific trade will turn out. The risk you take on is something you decide before entering.

u24l1-2.prompt: First reality check: look at this real chart. What did the price do over the following sessions?
u24l1-2.explanation: Looking at the chart isn't enough to know for sure. That's why professionals decide beforehand how much they'll lose if they're wrong.

u24l1-3.prompt: Another real chart, with no name or date. Does it go up or down afterwards?
u24l1-3.explanation: Getting a single prediction right or wrong says little. What decides your long-term result is how much you risk on each attempt.

u24l1-4.prompt: Match the risk per trade with what you have left after 10 losses in a row.
u24l1-4.explanation: Each loss applies to what's left: 0.99¹⁰ ≈ 90.4 % and 0.9¹⁰ ≈ 34.9 %.

u24l1-5.prompt: You risk 2 % per trade and take 10 losses in a row. What percentage of the account do you have left? (round to one decimal place)
u24l1-5.explanation: 0.98¹⁰ ≈ 0.817 → you keep 81.7 %. To get back you'd need to gain 22.4 %.

u24l1-6.prompt: Pablo is right on 60 % of his trades, but he wins €50 when he's right and loses €150 when he's wrong. Laura is right only 40 % of the time, but wins €300 and loses €100. After 10 trades, who's doing better?
options: Laura, because her wins are worth more than her losses
It's a draw, both are right half the time on average
Pablo, because he's right more often
u24l1-6.explanation: The result depends on your win rate and also on how much you win and lose each time.
feedback: Laura: 4 × 300 − 6 × 100 = +€600. She's wrong more often, but her losses are small.
No: what matters is the size of each win and each loss, not just how many there are.
Pablo: 6 × 50 − 4 × 150 = −€300. Being right a lot doesn't save him.

u24l1-7.prompt: You can make money while being right on fewer than half of your trades.
u24l1-7.explanation: Yes, if what you win when you're right is quite a bit more than what you lose when you're wrong. You'll see it with expectancy.

u24l1-8.prompt: Do you control it or not?
options: Whether the company posts good results
How much I risk on the trade
What the market will do tomorrow
u24l1-8.explanation: Focus on what depends on you: risk, stop and number of trades.

u24l1-9.prompt: Quick one: you risk 10 % per trade and lose 10 in a row. How much do you have left?
u24l1-9.explanation: 0.9¹⁰ ≈ 34.9 %: you'd need to gain 187 % to get back.

u24l5-1.prompt: You buy at the last price after a bounce. Place the stop where the idea stops being valid.
u24l5-1.explanation: Below the last relevant low: if the price breaks it, the bounce has failed.

u24l5-2.prompt: Another real chart. Place a structural stop for this buy.
u24l5-2.explanation: Below the recent low, with a small margin for normal noise.

u24l5-3.prompt: A Spanish share. Place the stop with logic, not where it hurts.

u24l5-4.explanation: Higher highs and higher lows. In an uptrend, the stop on a buy usually goes below the latest higher low.

u24l5-5.prompt: In a sideways market, the stop on a buy at the bottom of the range goes below the range low. Tap that low. (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · September–November 2024)
u24l5-5.explanation: If the price breaks the floor of the range, the bounce idea no longer holds.

u24l5-9.explanation: If the price gaps down at the open, it fills at the first available price, which may be worse.
